[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Mixed Precision Training in TensorFlow: FP16 and BF16"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Mixed precision training is a technique used in deep learning to accelerate model training and reduce memory consumption. By utilizing both 16-bit and 32-bit floating-point types, you can maximize the performance of modern GPUs without sacrificing model accuracy."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding FP16 vs. BF16"},{"order":4,"type":"bullet_point","text":"FP16 (Half Precision): Uses 1 bit for sign, 5 bits for the exponent, and 10 bits for the mantissa. It offers high performance but has a limited dynamic range, often requiring loss scaling to prevent underflow."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"BF16 (Brain Floating Point): Uses 1 bit for sign, 8 bits for the exponent (same as FP32), and 7 bits for the mantissa. It matches the dynamic range of FP32, making loss scaling unnecessary in most cases."},{"order":6,"type":"subheading","text":"Enabling Mixed Precision in TensorFlow"},{"order":7,"type":"paragraph","text":"TensorFlow provides a global policy API through tf.keras.mixed_precision to easily configure mixed precision training. Below is how you set the policy to FP16."},{"order":8,"type":"code","text":"import tensorflow as tf

# Enable mixed precision policy for float16
policy = tf.keras.mixed_precision.Policy('mixed_float16')
tf.keras.mixed_precision.set_global_policy(policy)

print('Compute dtype: %s' % policy.compute_dtype)
print('Variable dtype: %s' % policy.variable_dtype)"},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"Using BF16 on Supported Hardware"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"If you are using modern hardware accelerators like Google Cloud TPUs or NVIDIA Ampere (and newer) GPUs, you can use the bfloat16 format instead."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"import tensorflow as tf

# Enable mixed precision policy for bfloat16
policy = tf.keras.mixed_precision.Policy('mixed_bfloat16')
tf.keras.mixed_precision.set_global_policy(policy)

print('Compute dtype: %s' % policy.compute_dtype)
print('Variable dtype: %s' % policy.variable_dtype)"},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"Building and Compiling the Model"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"Once the global policy is set, any Keras layers you instantiate will automatically use mixed precision weights and activations. Ensure that your final output layer remains in float32 for numerical stability."},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"import tensorflow as tf

model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(512, activation='relu', input_shape=(784,)),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(512, activation='relu'),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(10, dtype='float32') # Final layer in float32
])

optimizer = tf.keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=0.001)

# If using mixed_float16, wrap the optimizer with LossScaleOptimizer
if tf.keras.mixed_precision.global_policy().name == 'mixed_float16':
    optimizer = tf.keras.mixed_precision.LossScaleOptimizer(optimizer)

model.compile(optimizer=optimizer,
              loss=tf.keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True),
              metrics=['accuracy'])"},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"Summary"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"Mixed precision training significantly reduces memory usage and speeds up training on compatible GPUs and TPUs. Use mixed_float16 with loss scaling for standard GPUs, and mixed_bfloat16 for supported TPUs and newer GPU architectures."}]
